replies:
If you have no symptoms and no known risk factors, major health organizations like the U.S. Preventive Services Task Force (USPSTF) do not currently recommend routine, population-wide oral cancer screening for adults without symptoms. The evidence is still unclear about whether screening in symptom-free people reduces the risk of dying from oral cancer.

That said, the answer isn’t a simple “no” for everyone, because:

- **Routine dental visits already include a basic oral cancer screening.** Most dentists and dental hygienists visually inspect your mouth, lips, tongue, and throat for any abnormal areas during a regular check-up and cleaning. This quick, painless exam is often done without you even realizing it. So if you’re seeing a dentist regularly, you’re essentially getting screened.
- **Risk factors matter.** If you use tobacco (cigarettes, cigars, chewing tobacco, etc.), drink alcohol heavily, or have a history of HPV (human papillomavirus) infection, you’re at higher risk. In those cases, many dentists and doctors will be more intentional about screening and may recommend more frequent or thorough exams.
- **Screening is more than just looking for symptoms you can feel.** Early oral cancers can be very subtle—small white or red patches, tiny ulcers that don’t hurt, or areas that are visible but not painful. You might have no symptoms at all in the earliest, most treatable stages.

**What does an oral cancer screening involve?**  
Typically, it’s a visual and tactile exam: the provider looks at the inside of your lips, gums, cheeks, roof and floor of the mouth, tongue, and back of the throat, and feels for lumps or rough spots. Some use additional tools (like special lights or dyes), but these aren’t yet proven to improve outcomes better than a good conventional exam.

**Bottom line:**  
If you have no symptoms and are at average risk, there’s no need to seek out a special screening test beyond your normal dental check-ups. If you haven’t seen a dentist in a while, making an appointment for a routine exam is a good idea for multiple reasons—and it will include an oral cancer check as part of that visit. If you have risk factors, talk to your dentist or primary care provider about how often and how carefully you should be screened.

Always feel free to ask your dentist to do an oral cancer exam if you want extra reassurance—it’s quick, non-invasive, and can be part of your routine care.
